newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia hopes EU meeting won't snag on Burma, Timor.
newsitem.headline: Asia hopes EU meeting won't snag on Burma, Timor.

text.p: Asian and European nations hold two sets of top-level meetings this week which officials hope will focus on strengthening economic ties and not stray into the touchy issue of human rights in Burma and East Timor.
If Burma or East Timor are raised, the meetings could easily dissolve into acrimony, and, in the case of East Timor, could spark a walkout by Indonesia.
The seven-nation Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) holds its 12th ministerial meeting with the European Union on February 13-14.
This will be followed by the first Asia-Europe Foreign Ministers Meeting (ASEM) on February 15, which will also involve ministers from China, South Korea and Japan.

Officials say neither meeting is likely to stray far from bland communiques over future economic ties but some diplomats have said they are worried Europe may push issues such as human rights, where there are sharp differences between the two blocs.

The EU has been critical of the human rights record of Burma's military government, with which ASEAN has close links. European states have also criticised Indonesia's human rights record in the former Portuguese colony of East Timor, which Indonesia invaded in 1975 and annexed the next year.
Indonesia has said it will walk out of the EU-ASEAN meeting if the subject of East Timor is raised.
But a senior Asian official said on Tuesday, he thought both sides wanted to avoid these contentious issues.

"We will not allow one or two difficult issues to distract our attention from the positive agenda," said the official, who declined to be identified. "My hope is that we can take stock of what we have achieved up to now and also review the potential of greater things to come.
"I am just hoping that officials and ministers on both sides will see that there is tremendous potential for a positive agenda and not allow our different perspectives to wreck the meeting," he said.
ASEAN groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.

Burma is a particularly sensitive subject to ASEAN because the group has already agreed to grant Rangoon membership at the same time it admits Cambodia and Laos. No date has yet been set for the entry of the three countries.
Singapore Foreign Minister Shanmugam Jayakumar stressed on Monday that a key ASEAN principle was not to interfere in the domestic politics of other countries.
He said the Asia-Europe meetings this week should avoid conflict on areas such as Burma and East Timor.

"We realise and acknowledge that our two regions have different perceptions on democracy and development...However this has not been a serious obstacle to both sides cooperating on many areas of common interest," Jayakumar said in a written response to questions from Reuters.
